title: Why Is New York Covering Up Test Scores?
author: Mark Schneider
summary: Mark Schneider, former commissioner of the National Center for Education Statistics and director of the Institute of Education Sciences, backs Eva Moskowitz's lawsuit against New York's Education Department for blocking the release of school-level AP exam results. He explains that the state's order barred the College Board from sharing verified AP data with U.S. News, causing Success Academy schools to plummet in rankings despite far higher AP pass rates than typical schools. Schneider calls the state's student privacy rationale a canard, since aggregate data are not sensitive, and agrees that the restriction may violate the First Amendment. He argues the real motive is that New York's traditional public schools are failing, as NAEP results with rising below-basic reading shares show. Drawing on decades of experience, he concludes that state leaders and teachers unions often bury bad outcomes, and that hindering data flow protects bad teachers and bad schools.
points: New York's education commissioner barred the College Board from sharing AP data, citing student privacy.
Ninety-five percent of Success Academy's 2026 graduates passed at least three AP exams.
Thirty-five percent of New York eighth graders scored below basic in reading on the 2024 NAEP, up five points since 2022.
Schneider argues aggregate school data are far less sensitive than individual student records.
He contends that state leaders and unions share an interest in suppressing data that could spur accountability reforms.
quotes: Education stakeholders across the board need the data to make informed choices about New York’s schools. Parents need the data to decide where to enroll their children and to gauge how well schools are performing. Policymakers need the data for accountability.
As Moskowitz argues, the state’s invocation of student privacy is a canard: Aggregate data, the kind she is seeking, are not nearly as sensitive as individual student records.
I believe the state is withholding the data because its traditional public schools are not doing their job.
During those years, I learned an ugly truth: Far too many state leaders work hard to bury bad outcomes.

Entrenched interests, especially teachers’ unions, also have a stake in suppressing these data, since bad outcomes can spur changes to accountability policy, and such changes almost always cut against teacher autonomy and job protections.
Hindering the flow of data only serves to protect bad teachers and bad schools. Perhaps good politics, but terrible policy.
